characterization_methods.key_findings: Both the 0Al and 1.3Al steels exhibit tempered martensitic structures with differently oriented packets.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: specimens cut from impact specimens, ground, polished and etched with 4 vol% nitric acid-ethanol solution
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize the tempered martensitic microstructure and martensitic units/packet sizes

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: JEM-F200; imaging at 200 KV accelerating voltage; thin foils electropolished by double-jet thinning at 30 V and −25 °C using a 10 vol% perchloric acid alcohol solution
characterization_methods.key_findings: Tempered martensitic laths with high dislocation densities and sharp lath boundaries; thin films of retained austenite at lath boundaries (indexed (110)γ adjacent to (111)M, K–S relationship); needle-like ε-carbides 100–500 nm long and 3–10 nm wide within the laths.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: thin foils extracted from the matrix, ground to 50 μm, punched into Φ3 mm discs
characterization_methods.purpose: Characterize tempered martensite laths, retained austenite and ε-carbides
characterization_methods.technique: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with selected area electron diffraction (SAED)

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Bruker e-Flash FS detector on the SEM; 20 KV accelerating voltage, 0.1 μm step size; Aztec Crystal v2.1 software
characterization_methods.key_findings: Average prior austenite grain size 26.1 ± 9.4 μm for 0Al; average KAM value of 1.16° with inhomogeneous strain distribution near the main crack (red/yellow high-KAM regions adjacent to the crack, large blue undeformed areas nearby).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: specimens 10 × 10 × 5 mm^3, mechanically polished with 0.02 μm colloidal silica suspension
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure prior austenite grain and martensitic unit sizes; kernel average misorientation (KAM) near main cracks

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Rigaku D/Max-2550 with Co radiation source operated at 40 KV and 150 mA
characterization_methods.key_findings: Small amount of retained austenite (1.0 % for 0Al); dislocation density ~2.01 × 10^15 m^-2 for the 0Al steel; peaks (110)α, (111)γ, (200)α, (200)γ, (211)α, (220)α.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: scans from 20° to 110° at a scanning rate of 2°/min
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine retained austenite content (direct comparison method) and dislocation density (Williamson-Hall method)

analytical_models.equation_role: Estimate lattice strain ε and apparent crystallite size D from XRD peak broadening, then dislocation density ρ
analytical_models.model_note: Equation (2): Δ2θcosθ/λ = 0.9/D + 2εsinθ/λ; ρ = 2√3ε/(D·b). Fitted using the (110)M, (200)M and (211) peaks for the 0Al steel.

computational_details.simulation_method: Williamson-Hall analysis of XRD peak broadening

analytical_models.equation_role: Compute conditional plane-strain fracture toughness KQ
analytical_models.model_note: KQ = (FQ·S / (B·W^(3/2))) × f(a/W), where f depends on the a/W ratio.

computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: three-point bending; loading rate 38 KN/min; specimen thickness 25 mm, width 50 mm, 3 mm fatigue pre-crack at notch tip
computational_details.simulation_method: ASTM E399 conditional fracture toughness (KQ) calculation with three-point bending

defect_interactions.interaction_type: transgranular crack propagation with deflection at block boundaries
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: In the 0Al steel cracks crossed packets and deviated along or through blocks; the main crack in fracture-toughness specimens propagated almost straight with minimal deviations, suggesting faster crack growth, and was rapidly blunted upon penetrating the matrix.

interfaces.phase_evolution: During low-temperature tempering at 180 °C, ε-carbides precipitate within the martensitic laths while a small amount of retained austenite remains (1.0 % for the 0Al steel).
interfaces.slip_behavior: ε-carbides promote dislocation cell formation through bypassing; dense packet boundaries and low-angle boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion; dislocations distributed relatively non-homogeneously compared with the 1.3Al steel.

processing_steps.method: vacuum induction melting followed by vacuum arc remelting (VIM + VAR), then forging
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: VIM + VAR into 500 kg ingots, subsequently forged into Φ170 mm billets; specimens for microstructural and mechanical characterization were extracted from the quarter-radius position.
Solution treatment at 970 °C for 1 h to dissolve carbides, with water quenching after the step.
Low-temperature tempering at 180 °C for 2 h with water quenching, producing the sample denoted 0Al,2 h.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Three tests per sample condition were performed; both specimen surfaces and notches were mechanically polished.
measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: tensile: diameter 5 mm, gauge length 25 mm; Charpy U-notch: 10 × 10 × 55 mm^3; fracture toughness: thickness 25 mm, width 50 mm with 3 mm fatigue pre-crack

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress-strain curve for 0Al,2 h (dashed blue curve) peaks near 1900–1950 MPa around strain 8–9 and extends to strain ~14 ending near 1250–1300 MPa

grain_structure.grain_size_distribution: prior austenite grain d_a = 26.1 ± 9.4 μm; martensitic packet d_p = 3.4 ± 0.8 μm; martensitic block d_b = 0.9 ± 0.2 μm; martensitic lath d_l = 0.24 ± 0.07 μm

phases_present.morphology: lath-shaped tempered martensite with sharp lath boundaries and high dislocation density
needle-like, aligned along a common crystallographic direction

precipitates.distribution: uniformly precipitated within the martensitic laths, aligned along a common crystallographic direction

microstructure_list.region: matrix (bulk, specimens taken from quarter-radius position)

structures.overall_structure: Tempered martensitic structure: lath-shaped tempered martensite with sharp lath boundaries and high dislocation density; thin films of retained austenite at lath boundaries; needle-like ε-carbides uniformly precipitated within the laths. A small amount of retained austenite (1.0 %) remains after tempering.

unmapped_findings: Charpy U-notch impact absorption energy KU2 = 65 ± 3 J for 0Al,2 h (Table 2 / Fig. 1b).

Instrumented Charpy load-deflection for the 0Al steel (Fig. 7b): peak load P_m = 39.7 KN at a deflection of 2.06 mm, crack initiation energy E_i = 45.0 J, crack propagation energy E_p = 17.4 J, and integrated KU2 = 62.4 J; the 0Al steel showed 17.4 J crack propagation energy, 4.6 J less than the 1.3Al steel.
Shear fracture area of 36.8 % measured for the 0Al steel impact specimen (the 1.3Al steel gave 42.9 %).

Average kernel average misorientation (KAM) of 1.16° near the impact fracture surface in the 0Al steel, with an inhomogeneous strain distribution (red/yellow high-KAM regions adjacent to the main crack and large blue undeformed areas in the adjacent matrix); KAM colour-bar class fractions: 0.0–0.7° 23.8 %, 0.7–1.4° 47.5 %, 1.4–2.1° 19.8 %, 2.1–2.8° 6.5 %, 2.8–3.5° 2.4 %.

The 0Al steel lacks NiAl clusters; the NiAl cluster (B2, ~4.88 × 10^24 m^-3, equivalent radius 0.57 nm) and Si/Cr/Mo co-segregation observations (Figs. 5–6) pertain only to the 1.3Al steel and are therefore not attributed to this sample.
